name: Gareth Diaz

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for your time, Gareth. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and what you say stays anonymous. Could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm an operator at a soft drinks bottling plant, on the filling line. Empty bottles come in on a conveyor, my filler fills them, the capper screws the lids on, and then they go off to labelling. I watch the fill levels, top up the cap hopper, clear jams, and help with changeovers when we switch from one flavour or bottle size to another. I've been there about eighteen months, so I'm still the one who gets sent to fetch the right change parts.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you enjoy, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I enjoy a good changeover, when we get it done in forty minutes instead of an hour and the shift manager actually says well done. What wears me out is the sticky floor and the noise, you go home with your ears ringing even with plugs. My partner Sian's a dental nurse, so she's got normal hours and I'm on shifts, but we make it work. I've got a forklift licence too, which comes in handy when the warehouse is short.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say fair enough, it was overhyped. Plenty of things are. I'd probably say it in the group chat with the five-a-side lads and then we'd move on to the football.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's fine for me. My job stays roughly the same, and I can keep working my way up to line lead in a few years. No drama.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing what I'm doing. Sian and I put money aside every month, we've got about three months saved, and we're slowly building a house deposit. I'd keep doing that. I might use the AI apps a bit more for the boring stuff, like writing up my review.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. It's just normal life.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Even in a plateau, some routine tasks get automated. What would you expect at the plant?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not much. Maybe the scheduling, deciding which flavour runs when. That's a bloke in the office with a spreadsheet right now. If a computer did it better, we'd have fewer changeovers, which would be nice actually.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would that bother you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not really. I'd find it handy. I use one of those chatbot apps now and then, I used it to plan our holiday last year and it was decent. I'm not going to fall in love with it, but it's a tool.

S0.say: Fair enough, it was overhyped, like plenty of things. I'd say it in the five-a-side group chat and we'd move on to the football.
S0.think: It's fine for me because my job stays roughly the same and I can work up to line lead. No drama.
S0.do: Keeps working and saving monthly with Sian from about three months towards a house deposit. Uses AI apps a little more for paperwork like his review. Welcomes better scheduling if it means fewer changeovers.
S0.quote: I'm not going to fall in love with it, but it's a tool.
S0.fieldNote: Gareth is relaxed and unbothered by a plateau, with a clear sense of his next step to line lead. He uses AI occasionally for practical things and treats it as a tool. Notably he'd welcome automation in scheduling because it would make his own shifts easier.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say some jobs go, some come, that's always been the way. Companies have to stay competitive or everyone's out of work. But they should train people properly, I'd say that too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd be a bit worried. My filler's already pretty automatic. The next step is a line that does its own changeovers, and then what's my job? But someone has to maintain it, so I'd want to be that someone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask my manager in the first few months what the plan is and whether I can get on the maintenance training. I'd probably do an electrical course at the college, once I'd seen a couple of the lads do it and come out with better jobs. And I'd push our savings up a bit, so we've got options.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit uneasy. Not losing sleep, but thinking about it on the drive home.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd wait until you'd seen a couple of lads do the course. Why wait?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's me, isn't it. I don't want to be the guinea pig. When someone I know has done it and it worked, I'll do it too. It's not that I'm scared, I just like to see proof.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's your backup plan if the line doesn't need you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The forklift ticket. Warehouses always need drivers, at least for now. So if the line went, I'd have something to fall back on while I sorted myself out.

S1.say: Some jobs go and some come, and companies have to stay competitive. But they should train people properly.
S1.think: My filler is already fairly automatic, and the next step is a line that changes over itself. Someone has to maintain it, so I'd want to be that someone.
S1.do: Asks his manager in the first few months about the plan and maintenance training. Takes an electrical course at the college once colleagues have shown it pays off. Builds savings a bit and keeps his forklift licence as a fallback.
S1.feel: Uneasy, thinking about it on the drive home but not losing sleep.
S1.quote: I don't want to be the guinea pig. When someone I know has done it and it worked, I'll do it too.
S1.fieldNote: His 'see proof first' approach is consistent and self-aware. He's balanced in public, sympathetic to companies but expecting training. The forklift licence gives him a real sense of a safety net that the other options don't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm not sure anyone can stop it, but the government had better have a plan for all the people out of work. That's not left or right, that's just common sense. Otherwise you've got a mess.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, the forklift backup's gone too, robots do that in this picture. So I'd be twenty-nine with no fallback. Sian's job might hold a bit longer, people don't love a robot in their mouth, but not forever.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd cut back straight away, no holiday, cancel the gym and the streaming stuff. We'd freeze the house deposit and keep that money as our emergency fund instead. I'd try to get any job that looked like it'd last a bit longer, maybe something where people want a person, like working at the hospital.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty alarmed. Like the ground's moving and I haven't worked out which way to jump.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the first big plan you'd drop?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The house. We've been saving for two years. If it all goes in 2028, I'm not signing a mortgage for twenty-five years on a job that won't exist. That deposit would be what we live on instead.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you talk to Sian about it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Proper scared, but not to her. I'd say we've got the deposit money and we'll be all right for a while. That's true, it's just not the whole truth.

S2.say: I'm not sure anyone can stop it, but the government had better have a plan for people out of work. That's not left or right, just common sense.
S2.think: Even my forklift backup goes, so I'd be twenty-nine with no fallback. Sian's job might last a bit longer because people don't love a robot in their mouth, but not forever.
S2.do: Cuts back straight away on holidays, gym and streaming. Freezes the house deposit and treats it as an emergency fund. Looks for work that might last longer, such as a hospital job where people want a person.
S2.feel: Alarmed, unsure which way to jump, and hiding the worst of it from Sian.
S2.quote: I'm not signing a mortgage for twenty-five years on a job that won't exist.
S2.fieldNote: Losing the forklift fallback is what breaks his calm, because it was his safety net. He switches the house deposit into an emergency fund, a concrete and sensible move. He admitted he'd tell Sian a comforting half-truth.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got five years, so let's get on with it. Retrain, save, sort yourself out. I wouldn't moan about it online, I'd just get on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years means I could do the maintenance training and get a few years out of it. Not forever, but it's something. And it'd mean better money to save.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sign up for the electrical course in the first year, even if I hadn't seen anyone else do it yet, because the clock's running. I'd push the savings hard, maybe to eight months. And we'd hold off on the house until we saw what was happening.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but it's the kind you can work with.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Earlier you said you don't like being the guinea pig. Here you'd go first. What changed?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yeah, fair point. But with five years you can't wait for proof. The proof turns up when it's too late.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If you could only pick one thing to focus on in those five years, what would it be?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably still the maintenance. And then after, I honestly don't know. I'm not a big planner past a few years. Sian's the planner.

S3.say: We've got five years, so let's get on with it: retrain, save and sort yourself out. I wouldn't moan online.
S3.think: Five years means I could do the maintenance training and get a few years out of it. Not forever, but better money to save.
S3.do: Signs up for the electrical course in the first year without waiting for proof. Pushes savings towards eight months. Holds off on buying the house until things become clearer.
S3.feel: Anxious but in a workable way.
S3.quote: With five years you can't wait for proof. The proof turns up when it's too late.
S3.fieldNote: When I named his 'proof first' habit, he saw why it fails under a short clock and changed course. He's focused on a few years ahead and openly hands longer planning to Sian. Holding off the house purchase is his main life change here.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years, I'd say that's loads of time if people are sensible. I'd tell the lads to start thinking about it, but no need to panic. I'd probably share an article or two.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd feel like I've got a fair shot. Get the maintenance skills, maybe move into something like installing these systems. And by 2036 we'd have bought a house and hopefully paid a chunk off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd watch how the first couple of years went, then do the electrical course once a few people had done it, like I said before. I'd keep saving and probably put a bit into a pension or shares, in case the robot companies are where the money ends up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. It's a long way off, but you know it's coming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you still buy the house in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yeah, I would. Ten years is long enough that buying in a couple of years and paying extra each month makes sense. Five years wouldn't be.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the extra time change for you, compared with five years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It gives me time to be me, I suppose. Wait, watch, then move. With five years I'd have to rush, and I don't do my best stuff rushed.

S4.say: Ten years is loads of time if people are sensible, so no need to panic. I'd tell the lads to start thinking about it and share an article or two.
S4.think: I'd have a fair shot: get maintenance skills, maybe move into installing these systems. By 2036 we'd have bought a house and paid a chunk off.
S4.do: Watches the first couple of years, then takes the electrical course once others have done it. Keeps saving and puts some into a pension or shares in case robot firms are where the money goes. Buys a house in a couple of years and overpays each month.
S4.feel: Uneasy; it's far off but definitely coming.
S4.quote: With five years I'd have to rush, and I don't do my best stuff rushed.
S4.fieldNote: The long warning lets him return to his natural wait-then-move style, and he says so plainly. His idea of buying shares in robot companies was a practical hedge. The house is back on, with a plan to overpay the mortgage.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. No time to see what works, no fallback, and the house goes out the window. What would help is some sort of bridge, like your wages topped up for a year while you retrain, and companies being honest early about what they're bringing in.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe how normal people actually find out about this stuff. Most of the lads get it from short videos on their phones, half of it rubbish. If someone sensible just told us straight, we'd make better choices.

headlineQuote: If someone sensible just told us straight, we'd make better choices.
portrait: Gareth is a 27-year-old junior operator on the filling line at a soft drinks bottling plant, living with his partner Sian, a dental nurse, and saving for a house deposit. He's pragmatic and middle-of-the-road, uses AI apps now and then, and likes to see proof before he moves; his forklift licence is his safety net. A plateau or steady change barely shakes him, but fast AGI alarms him because even the forklift fallback disappears. Five years makes him drop his 'wait for proof' habit, while ten years lets him wait, then move, and still buy the house.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because there's no time to see what works, no fallback job, and the house plans collapse.
whatWouldHelp: A bridge such as wages topped up for a year while retraining, and companies being honest early about what they're bringing in.
